home-remodeling.local_heading: Acre lots, good bones, better plans
intro_paragraphs: Pinecrest was built out in the 1950s and 60s as ranch houses on acre lots, and that DNA still runs from North Pinecrest down to Devonwood. The teardown crews have been busy here for years, but plenty of owners look at a solid CBS ranch under mature oaks and decide the bones are worth keeping. That is where we come in: full-gut remodels that open up low-slung layouts, raise the finish level to match the street, and keep the trees that made you buy the lot in the first place. In Kendall Park Estates and along Old Cutler Road, that math often beats new construction.

Permits run through the Village of Pinecrest Building and Planning Department, which reviews building, zoning, and tree protection under one roof. There is no Coral Gables-style board of architects here, but do not mistake that for a light touch: the village's tree ordinance guards the canopy, specimen trees need arborist review before anything moves, and every window, door, and roof assembly must carry Miami-Dade product approvals for the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone. We prepare complete digital submittals, sequence tree and zoning review alongside the building permit, and show up for every inspection.

A whole-home remodel in Pinecrest is a long relationship — months of trades working on a quiet street. We run it like professionals: a fixed written scope before demolition starts, a supervisor on site daily, floors and finishes protected, and neighbors who barely notice us beyond the dumpster. One team stays accountable from the first estimate to the final walk-through, backed by more than 20 years building in South Florida and over 150 remodels and additions delivered.

faqs.q: Should I remodel my Pinecrest ranch or tear it down and build new?
faqs.a: It depends on the structure, the layout, and how much of the house you actually like. A solid CBS ranch with a good roofline can absorb a dramatic remodel for meaningfully less than new construction, and it keeps mature trees that a teardown often sacrifices. If the footprint is simply wrong for how you live, new construction may win. We will walk it with you and give you a straight answer either way.

faqs.q: How long does whole-home remodel permitting take in Pinecrest?
faqs.a: The Village of Pinecrest reviews plans digitally, and timelines depend on scope — structural changes, tree work, and revision rounds all add time. We will not quote you a fake number, but we will tell you this: complete, well-prepared submittals move measurably faster than optimistic ones. We sequence engineering, tree permits, and the building application so reviews run in parallel wherever the village allows it.

faqs.q: Can you raise the ceilings in a 1960s ranch house?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Many ranch-era homes hide usable height above the flat ceiling, and vaulting to the roofline can transform the main living spaces. It is structural work — engineering, permits, inspections — not a weekend drywall project. Where the roof framing will not allow it, we get a similar effect with wider openings, taller doors, and glass, and we will tell you which house you own before you commit.

faqs.q: Will Pinecrest's tree ordinance affect my remodel?
faqs.a: If the work touches the yard, probably. Pinecrest requires permits to remove or relocate trees, and specimen trees get reviewed by the village arborist, with replacement planting required when removal is approved. For interior remodels this rarely matters, but additions, driveways, and equipment placement all interact with root zones. We design around the canopy from the start, because in Pinecrest the trees are half the point of the property.

faqs.q: What does a high-end whole-home remodel cost in Pinecrest?
faqs.a: Less than a comparable new build, more than a coat of paint, and heavily dependent on structural scope and finish level. Full-gut remodels of acre-lot homes are serious construction projects, and we price them line by line in a fixed written scope rather than a vague allowance that grows later. We are not the cheapest bid in Miami-Dade, and we are comfortable saying so.

kitchen-remodeling.h1: Kitchens built for how Pinecrest entertains
kitchen-remodeling.hero_sub: Custom kitchen remodeling for Pinecrest homes — cabinetry built to the millimeter, stone counters, real islands, and the permits and licensed trades (Lic. CGC1539072) that let you move walls and gas lines legally.
kitchen-remodeling.local_heading: From galley kitchen to gathering room
intro_paragraphs: The original Pinecrest kitchen was a galley tucked behind the carport, sized for one cook and a wall phone. That is not how anyone in North Pinecrest or Suniland lives now. The kitchens we build here anchor the whole house: a ten-foot island, cabinetry run to the ceiling, and sight lines across the family room and out to the pool. Whether yours is an original ranch off Killian Drive or a 1990s rebuild that already feels dated, the kitchen is usually the room where a remodel earns its keep.

Moving a sink, a range, or a wall means a permit from the Village of Pinecrest Building and Planning Department, which reviews plans digitally and inspects electrical, plumbing, and mechanical work separately. Many Pinecrest kitchens also need a panel upgrade — a 1960s service was never sized for double ovens, an induction range, and a wine column running at once. We handle the load calculations, the licensed trades, and the inspections, so the paperwork matches the kitchen instead of haunting your future sale.

Kitchens are where high-end shows, or does not. We build to a fixed written scope with cabinetry shop drawings approved before anything is ordered, stone slabs you have personally seen and tagged, and a site supervisor checking reveals and alignments daily. Dust containment keeps the rest of the house livable, deliveries are staged so your driveway is not a warehouse, and one PGX team stays accountable from estimate through warranty.

faqs.q: How much does a custom kitchen remodel cost in Pinecrest?
faqs.a: Cabinetry and stone drive the number more than square footage does. A fully custom kitchen with layout changes, new electrical, and slab counters is a significant investment, and in this market it is usually the highest-impact room in the house. We price every line — cabinets, stone, appliances, trades — in a fixed written scope, so you decide with real numbers instead of allowances.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to remodel my kitchen in Pinecrest?
faqs.a: If the project moves plumbing, electrical, gas, or walls — and almost every real kitchen remodel does — yes, through the Village of Pinecrest Building and Planning Department. A straight swap of cabinets and counters may not need one, but that is rarely the project people call us for. Permitted work protects your insurance position and your resale story, and inspections catch problems while they are still cheap.

faqs.q: Can you remove the wall between the kitchen and the living room?
faqs.a: Usually. In ranch-era Pinecrest homes that wall is often load-bearing, which means an engineered header or beam, a permit, and inspections — all routine for us. The result is the open kitchen-living-pool sight line these houses were secretly built for. We confirm what the wall is doing before design begins, so the plan you fall in love with is one that can actually be built.

faqs.q: My house still has its original electrical panel. Is that a problem for a new kitchen?
faqs.a: Very likely. A 1960s service was sized for one oven and a percolator, not induction cooking, double refrigeration, and a wine column. We run the load calculation early; if the panel or service needs upgrading, it goes in the written scope up front. If we find aluminum branch wiring, common in homes of that era, we will tell you plainly and price the correction honestly.

faqs.q: How long will I be without a kitchen?
faqs.a: For a full custom kitchen, plan on a stretch of weeks once demolition starts, with cabinetry lead time before that — custom boxes are built, not bought off a shelf. We compress the dark period by having cabinets, stone, and appliances confirmed before we open a single wall, and we can set up a functional temporary kitchen so the household keeps running.

bathroom-remodeling.title: Bathroom Remodeling — Pinecrest, FL | PGX Builders Group
bathroom-remodeling.meta_description: Bathroom remodeling in Pinecrest, FL: primary suites, frameless showers, waterproofing done to spec. Licensed and insured — call (786) 273-2524 for an estimate.
bathroom-remodeling.h1: Primary baths worth the square footage
bathroom-remodeling.hero_sub: Bathroom remodeling for Pinecrest homes — primary suites, frameless glass, freestanding tubs, and waterproofing done to spec. Licensed and insured (CGC1539072), permitted through the Village, and supervised every day it matters.
intro_paragraphs: A ranch-era Pinecrest house typically came with bathrooms that were generous for 1965 and comical now: a five-foot tub, a single sink, and tile the color of an avocado. Owners in South Pinecrest and Kendall Park Estates are rebuilding them as true primary suites — wet rooms with freestanding tubs, frameless showers lined in real slabs, double vanities with actual storage. Often the smartest move is borrowing space from an oversized closet or hallway, and on an acre lot there is usually somewhere for the square footage to come from.

Bathroom projects here are permitted through the Village of Pinecrest Building and Planning Department, with separate plumbing, electrical, and building inspections along the way. Two local realities matter. First, many original Pinecrest homes still run on cast-iron drain lines nearing the end of their service life — we camera-scope them rather than tile over a problem. Second, a fair number of properties in the village remain on septic systems, so relocating fixtures or adding a bathroom deserves a capacity check before plans are drawn.

Waterproofing is where bathroom remodels are won or lost, and it is invisible by the time anyone is admiring the marble. We put the whole assembly in writing — membranes, slopes, flood tests, movement joints — and a PGX supervisor verifies each step before tile goes on. Fixed scope, daily supervision, protected floors between the front door and the work zone, and one accountable team from first measurement to the warranty call you probably will not need.

faqs.q: How long does a primary bathroom remodel take in Pinecrest?
faqs.a: A true primary-suite rebuild — new layout, waterproofing, stone, glass — typically runs a few months from permit to final inspection, with village plan review before that. Small cosmetic refreshes go faster, but that is not usually what we are hired for. We give you a schedule tied to the written scope, and a supervisor who keeps the trades sequenced instead of stacked.

faqs.q: Should I replace the cast-iron drain lines during the remodel?
faqs.a: If your Pinecrest home predates the mid-1970s and still has original cast iron, almost certainly yes. We scope the lines before finalizing the contract; if they are failing, replacing them while the floor is already open costs a fraction of doing it after new marble is down. Nobody enjoys paying for pipe, but it is the least optional line item in an older bath.

faqs.q: Do bathroom remodels in Pinecrest require permits?
faqs.a: Yes, whenever plumbing, electrical, or structure changes — which covers essentially every remodel beyond swapping a faucet. Plans go through the Village of Pinecrest Building and Planning Department and the work is inspected in stages. That paper trail also protects you at appraisal and sale, when unpermitted bathroom work has a way of surfacing at the worst possible moment.

faqs.q: Can I add a bathroom if my house is on septic?
faqs.a: Often yes, but the septic system's capacity has to support it, and that gets evaluated before permits are issued — bedroom and fixture counts matter to the health review. Plenty of Pinecrest lots still run on septic, so this comes up regularly. We check it during the first site visit; if the system needs attention, you will know before design money is spent, not after.

faqs.q: What does a high-end bathroom remodel cost?
faqs.a: The range is wide because the choices are. Stone selection, glass, fixtures, and how far the plumbing moves all swing the number more than the room's size does. A gut renovation of a primary bath is a five-figure project at minimum in this market, and often well beyond with slab work and custom glass. We put every selection in a fixed written price before demolition.

bathroom-remodeling.cta_sub: Show us the bathroom that annoys you daily. We'll design the one that will not — priced in writing, in English o en español.

home-additions.h1: Room to grow on an acre
home-additions.hero_sub: Home additions across Pinecrest — rear extensions, second stories, and in-law suites engineered into ranch-era homes. Fully permitted through the Village and built by a licensed general contractor (CGC1539072) with daily site supervision.
home-additions.local_heading: Why Pinecrest was made for additions
intro_paragraphs: An acre lot forgives a lot of ambition. While owners on smaller Miami lots fight for every setback inch, Pinecrest families in North Pinecrest, Devonwood, and along Ludlam Road have room for a real rear extension, a detached studio, or a full second story — often without crowding the pool or the oaks. The village's estate zoning keeps lots large and neighbors distant, which is exactly why a well-designed Pinecrest home addition can add serious living space without the house ever feeling bolted together.

Additions are reviewed by the Village of Pinecrest Building and Planning Department, and two site issues usually shape the design before aesthetics do. Tree protection comes first: the village permits every significant removal and takes its specimen trees seriously, so we site additions around protected canopy rather than through it. Septic comes second: many Pinecrest lots still rely on septic systems, and an addition that adds bedrooms triggers a capacity review. We flag both in week one, not at plan review.

Structurally, adding to a 1960s ranch is real engineering: existing footings verified, tie beams upgraded, new work doweled and tied into old until the joint disappears. That is our home turf. PGX has spent more than 20 years building in South Florida, every addition is fully permitted and inspected, and a supervisor is on your site daily while your family keeps living in the house. One written scope, one accountable team, from first sketch to last inspection.

faqs.q: Do I need Village approval for an addition in Pinecrest?
faqs.a: Yes. Additions go through the Village of Pinecrest Building and Planning Department for zoning, building, and tree review — setbacks, lot coverage, and protected canopy all get checked against the plans. It is a thorough process but a rational one, and complete submittals with real engineering move through it far better than hopeful sketches. We prepare the full package and attend every inspection.

faqs.q: Will the tree rules decide where my addition can go?
faqs.a: They will have a vote. Pinecrest permits tree removals individually and gives specimen trees arborist-level scrutiny, with replacement planting required when removals are approved. In practice we treat major oaks as fixed points and design the addition around them — which usually produces a better courtyard, terrace, or window anyway. Fighting the canopy in Pinecrest is a losing strategy; designing with it is not.

faqs.q: Is a second story better than moving to a bigger house?
faqs.a: Frequently, yes — if the existing structure can take it. We verify foundations and upgrade tie beams as needed, and the engineering is settled before anyone commits. You keep the acre, the trees, the school zone, and the neighbors you like, and you gain a full floor. When the structure or the budget argues otherwise, we will say so and look at a ground-level extension instead.

faqs.q: What happens to my septic system when we add bedrooms?
faqs.a: Adding bedrooms triggers a review of septic capacity, because system sizing is tied to bedroom count. Many Pinecrest properties still operate on septic, so this is a normal part of addition planning here, not a nasty surprise. Sometimes the existing system passes; sometimes it needs modification. We identify which case you are in during the first site evaluation, before the drawings get expensive.

faqs.q: Can my family live in the house during the addition?
faqs.a: Usually, yes — one of the quiet advantages of an acre lot. We can typically isolate the work zone, keep the existing house weathertight until the connection is opened, and schedule the loud, dusty phases with your household in mind. There are a few days in every addition when you will want dinner out. We will tell you which days those are.

outdoor-living.local_heading: An acre of yard is a design brief
intro_paragraphs: Pinecrest backyards are the point. The village grew up around Pinecrest Gardens and its canopy of oaks and banyans, and the best properties in South Pinecrest and along Old Cutler Road treat the outdoors as another wing of the house: a covered terrace with a summer kitchen, a pergola over the dining area, a driveway that arrives rather than merely parks. On an acre, outdoor living is not decorating — it is construction, with footings, gas, drainage, and electrical that should be permitted and built like the house itself.

Exterior work here runs through the Village of Pinecrest Building and Planning Department, and the canopy comes first: tree protection is written into the village code, so terraces, driveways, and pergolas get designed around root zones and protected specimens, not over them. Anything structural or roofed also has to meet High-Velocity Hurricane Zone requirements, meaning engineered footings and connections plus Miami-Dade approved products for any new openings. We handle the permits, the arborist coordination, and the inspections as one package.

Outdoor projects attract unlicensed crews the way pools attract leaves; Pinecrest deserves better. PGX builds exterior work on a fixed written scope with real drawings, supervises the site daily, and coordinates every trade that touches your house — stucco, paint, re-roof coordination, impact openings — so the exterior reads as one design instead of five subcontracts. We protect the landscaping and hardscape while we work, and we leave the site clean enough that the only evidence is the terrace.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a summer kitchen or pergola in Pinecrest?
faqs.a: Almost always. Structures, roofs, footings, gas lines, and electrical all require permits through the Village of Pinecrest Building and Planning Department, and anything roofed or enclosed must meet High-Velocity Hurricane Zone requirements. Unpermitted backyard structures are a classic problem at sale time in this village. We design, permit, and inspect the outdoor work with exactly the rigor the main house gets.

faqs.q: Can you build a terrace near the big oaks without hurting them?
faqs.a: That is the assignment on most Pinecrest lots. Root zones limit where footings and grade changes can go, and the village's tree protection rules back that up with permitting and arborist review. We plan structures around driplines, use footing layouts that respect the roots, and treat the canopy as the ceiling of the outdoor room. The oaks were here first; good design admits it.

faqs.q: Will a covered terrace hold up in a hurricane?
faqs.a: Built correctly, yes — that is what High-Velocity Hurricane Zone engineering is for. Footings, columns, connections, and roofing are all designed for Miami-Dade wind loads, and products for openings carry Miami-Dade approvals. The outdoor structures that fail in storms are overwhelmingly the ones built without engineering or permits. Ours are inspected at every stage, which is precisely the point.

faqs.q: Do you build pools too?
faqs.a: We build everything around the pool — terraces, summer kitchens, pergolas, drainage, lighting — and we coordinate with licensed pool contractors when a pool is part of the project, so sequencing and elevations actually line up. What we will not do is pretend one trade covers everything. One accountable team runs the project; specialists do what they are licensed to do.

faqs.q: How much should I budget for outdoor living work?
faqs.a: It scales with structure. A pergola is one conversation; a covered terrace with a full summer kitchen, gas, and electrical is genuine construction and priced like it. On Pinecrest acre lots the temptation is to phase everything separately — we usually recommend one master plan, built in stages if needed, so the driveway, terrace, and drainage agree with each other.
